items_missed: Never asked the customer's name. The only reason Jack knows it is that Scott spelled his own email ('SCO, T. T. K. L. 8787. @att.net') — Jack never said 'and who am I speaking with?' and never used the name once in 11.8 minutes.
No 'how are you today?' — the customer opened with 'Good morning Jack' and Jack went straight to 'For sure. What day were you looking to move?'
No agenda statement and no 'sound good?'. The call never got a roadmap or a timeframe, which is why the probe wandered between rooms, addresses, appliances, and back to addresses.

Stairs and floors never asked at either address — on a 2,062 sqft house with 15 large framed pieces, two flat-screen TVs, and a rowing machine. This is a direct hit to estimate accuracy: he priced 15–16 hours with no idea whether either home has a staircase.

Access and special considerations never asked — no parking, no walk distance, no narrow hallways or tight turns, no HOA. He committed to two trucks without knowing whether two trucks can stage at either address.

Storage was raised by the customer and dropped by the rep. Scott said plainly 'whether it's this address or it ends up going to storage. I don't know yet' and Jack replied 'Both yup' and moved on. No storage-stop probe, no second-stop pricing, no note that the destination could change — on a quote he then sent in writing.
Additional stops never asked, despite the destination itself being unresolved.
Box count never asked. He put '$300 in packing materials' on the estimate without a single box-quantity question, then hedged it with wardrobe pricing after the fact.

No moving-stressor question. Scott handed him the opening — 'I've got pictures on the wall... with like, really cool stuff in them that I would like packed. Well' and 'it's a street bike... they're expensive. So it needs to be taken care of' — and neither concern was reflected back or tied to anything.
What's-included list was partial: 'we will wrap everything and blankets and shrink wrap' but no gas, truck, taxes, insurance, bands, or tools.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned — on a Saturday move date, the day it matters most.

No itemized 'no hidden fees' pitch. 'The only additional fee whatsoever, it's just for packing materials' gestures at it but never names no credit card fees, no transportation fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees.

No sense-check after the clock/pricing block. The entire rate, minimum, proration, packing estimate, move-day estimate, and $6,000 total were delivered as one uninterrupted monologue and Scott's only responses inside it were 'Okay. Okay. Yeah.' Jack never asked 'does that make sense?'
Drive time between Mansfield and Grand Prairie never explained as billable time, and no trip-fee position stated either way.
Walk distance and equivalents (school bus reference) never used to frame the two-truck call.

Entire Save Your Ass section missing — no prep-equals-shorter-move framing, no consolidation examples, no 'take a carload' tip, no close. Worth noting the customer volunteered the opening himself: 'I'm 61 I'm he broken. I've done this before... I'll be your low maintenance customer for the day, I promise' and 'I might even take it myself' about the bike. A willing, experienced customer on a 15–16 hour time-based job was given nothing to do.

No booking attempt. Jack confirmed availability in the first minute ('Yeah, we do have availability there') and never came back to it. The call ended on 'I'll send this quote you know and we'd love to help you out my friend' — a fully quoted job with a known date and confirmed availability, left unbooked.
'No deposit required' never mentioned — the single strongest reason for Scott to say yes on the call instead of 'I'll get back to you shortly.'

No BOLDED-details framing for the confirmation email and no 'reply with any corrections' — on a call where the origin address had to be re-asked ('can you actually, tell me the starting address one more time my computer messed up') and the destination is admittedly provisional. This email needs a verify-and-reply ask more than most.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' and no hours or how-to-reach-us.
Customer's name used zero times — 'sir' twice and 'my friend' once instead.
No Ecobox or Sparefoot referral despite the customer explicitly raising a possible storage stop and a heavy full-service pack.

Insurance explanation strong but incomplete — he contrasted No Worries against 'not just a weight based thing which a lot of companies do' without ever naming the 60¢/lb baseline that makes the contrast land.
top_strength: The inventory probe is the best part of this call and it is genuinely good. Jack did not accept '2062 foot house' as an answer — he worked it room by room and asked the questions that actually move a packing estimate: 'Each one of those bedrooms is being used like, as a bedroom set like mattress box, spring, bed frame, night stands closet all that stuff'; then the office in detail; then the one that matters most, 'packing is, is typically the hardest thing to estimate over the phone... Would you describe the kitchen as lots of glass glassware and say like, every shelf on, in the, in every cabinet, on every shelf or do you think it's a little bit more minimal' — which got him a usable answer ('probably eighty percent of what you just described... a couple of cabinets full of'). He kept going into the rest of the house, the patio, the appliances, specialty items, and the garage, and surfaced the rowing machine, the work bench, the shelving unit, 15 large framed pieces, three TVs, and the street bike. He then priced cleanly off that inventory: '$100 an hour per mover... four movers would be a $400 hourly rate,' full disassembly and reassembly included, packing at the same hourly rate plus roughly $300 in materials, wardrobes called out separately at '$18,' the 2.5-hour minimum, and 15-minute proration. He also volunteered two policies before being asked — 'we can take down any t.v.s, we just can't remount anything at the new place' and the motor-vehicle-on-the-truck boundary — and closed the differentiator he did use with real substance: 'we actually include up to 2000 dollars in protection that is in-house value based coverage... we just take care of it,' plus W-2 movers versus contract labor. Rapport was real, not performed: the baseball-memorabilia China cabinet got a laugh and 'Would you tell my wife, please,' and Scott ended the call with 'I greatly appreciate you.'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix, and it is the whole call: Jack built a quote worth about $6,000, confirmed the date was open in the first sixty seconds, earned real trust, and then never asked for the business. When Scott said 'Can you send me a written estimate on my email?' the answer needed to be 'Absolutely, sending it now — and Scott, since Saturday the 27th is open right now and there's no deposit to hold it, let me put your name on it while we're talking. If anything changes you just reply to that email and we'll move it, no charge.' Instead the close was 'we'd love to help you out my friend,' and a ready buyer with a confirmed date became a follow-up. Say the words 'no deposit' out loud on every quote — it is the cheapest close Einstein has and it was never spoken. Second priority: the Save Your Ass speech is worth more on this job than on almost any call this week, because it is 15–16 billable hours and Scott openly offered to help ('I'll be your low maintenance customer for the day, I promise'). He should have heard 'Here's how you knock real money off this bill: every carload you take yourself is time we're not charging for — kids' stuff, garden tools, the loose things in drawers, and take that street bike yourself since you already offered. Anything you can consolidate into boxes or get off the walls before Friday is time back in your pocket. Does that make sense?' Third, and the one that will show up in the estimate-accuracy numbers: Jack quoted two trucks, four movers, and 15–16 hours without ever asking about stairs, parking, walk distance, or access at either address — and he let a stated storage possibility go by with 'Both yup.' Scott said out loud that the destination might be storage instead of Bonham Trail. A quote is now in writing that could be missing a second stop entirely. Before that email goes out today: confirm the destination, get the stairs and parking at both addresses, and get the storage question answered — those three answers are the difference between a $6,000 quote and a $6,000 actual. Also worth building on: the No Worries pitch was strong but stopped one sentence short — add 'most companies pay 60 cents a pound, which on a flat-screen is about twelve dollars' and the contrast does the selling for him. Minor but real: the verbal tics are heavy ('gotcha' and 'cool' land well over thirty times combined), and the customer's name was never used once — 'Scott' three or four times would have made an already warm call feel personal.
phone_presence_notes: Easy, likeable energy that produced genuine rapport — the baseball-memorabilia exchange got 'Would you tell my wife, please' and the customer signed off with 'I greatly appreciate you' — held back from a 5 only by the never-once-used customer name and heavy filler ('gotcha,' 'cool, very cool') standing in for real acknowledgment.
audio_review_reason: The pricing and estimate block is materially garbled in the transcript — 'about 76 to maybe seven hours a packing,' 'Main another seven to maybe eight hours,' 'Brings me to about, you know, 1516 total moving hours' — so the exact hour ranges and the $6,000 total Jack actually quoted cannot be verified from text. Given this is a live estimate-accuracy case and the written quote follows, the audio should be checked against what lands in EMMA.
